title: Proteogenomics linked to histopathology identifies subtypes and progression biomarkers in malignant melanoma
projectDescription: In this study, proteogenomic analysis coupled with clinical histopathology revealed proteomic subtypes and identified candidate markers, which uncovered tumor biology related to patient survival. A total of 12,695 proteins and 45,356 phosphosites were quantified. This newly generated proteomic data was integrated with a previously published transcriptomic dataset from matched tumor specimens (Cirenajwis et al., 2015). Using consensus clustering, we could identify five melanoma subtypes, which were classified into extracellular, extracellular-immune, mitochondrial, mitochondrial-immune, and extracellular-mitochondrial categories according to/based on the annotations of their highly expressed proteins. The proteomic subtypes displayed differences in phenotype switching, immune surveillance, the levels of known melanoma markers, and were associated with survival. In addition, clinical parameters such as the expression of mutated BRAF V600E protein and the composition of the surrounding tumor microenvironment were found to be good independent indicators of prognosis. Lastly, validation of survival-related proteins in an independent cohort identified five candidate markers for predicting disease progression and patient survival (ADAM10, SCAI, CTNND1, CDK4, FGA). In conclusion, this study provides insights into the complex biology of melanoma while emphasizing/highlighting the importance of the tumor microenvironment. It also offers opportunities to find/indentify novel drug target candidates.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Treatment-naïve frozen lymph node metastases from 142 patients with malignant melanoma were sectioned and histopathologically examined. Global proteomics was performed by isobaric labeling with TMT 11-plex. Phosphoproteomic analysis was performed using DIA-MS following Fe(III)-NTA enrichment. The peptides were analyzed by nanoLC-MS/MS using an Ultimate 3000 UPLC coupled to a QExactive HF-X.
dataProcessingProtocol: Consensus clustering analyses Proteins commonly quantified across the samples (8125 proteins) with a tumor content above 30% were selected. Unsupervised-consensus hierarchical clustering analysis was performed with the 3000 proteins with the most variant expression levels (coefficient of variation > 0.36) using the Perseus software (v 1.6.14.0) (Tyanova et al., 2016). The clustering algorithm used k-means and Pearson correlation distance and average linkage. Five subgroups were identified as proteomic subtypes by visual inspection of the hierarchical tree. Subtypes and feature correlation Correlations between subtypes and clinico-histopathological features and transcriptomics subtypes were performed using Fisher’s exact test. Kruskal-Wallis test was performed on histological parameters including the contents of tumor cells, adjacent lymph nodes, tumor associated connective tissue and necrosis. Differential omics analysis To identify proteins, phosphosites and transcripts significantly expressed in each molecular subtype one-way ANOVA was performed using the TMT-based global proteomic, phosphoproteomic, and transcriptomic data, respectively. At least 30% of valid values were required for all datasets and the p-values were adjusted using the permutation-based FDR method. Survival biomarker analyses Two complementary supervised approaches to relate omics data to survival were applied. First, Outlier analysis, which treats survival as a binary variable. Second, the Cox analysis considers survival as a continuous variable. Samples with larger than 30% tumor cell content (n=111) were included in both analyses.
